summary:
## The Truth About KOA Campgrounds

Many common opinions about KOA—that they're all expensive, rundown, or have sites that are too close—are often generalizations. The reality is that KOA is a diverse network of campgrounds with widely varying quality, amenities, and pricing.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The vast majority of KOA's 500+ locations are independently owned and operated franchises. This model is the primary reason for the inconsistency in camper experiences, as each owner sets their own rules, prices, and maintenance standards.

## The KOA Franchise Model

Opening a KOA involves significant investment and adherence to corporate standards, which can influence nightly rates.

- **Initial Investment:** **$3.9 to $6.8 million** (excluding land costs).
- **Franchise Fees:**
  - `$40,000` initial fee.
  - `$1,700` annual fee.
  - `10%` of annual revenue given to KOA corporate for royalties and marketing.
- **Benefits for Owners:** Strong brand recognition, campground design assistance, management training at **KOA University**, and access to their proprietary reservation software (**K2**).

## KOA Campground Tiers

To help manage customer expectations, KOA categorizes its parks into three tiers, each with a minimum set of amenities.

- **KOA Journey:** Designed for convenient overnight stops. Must have pull-through RV sites, 50-amp service, clean bathrooms with hot water, and a KOA store.
- **KOA Holiday:** Intended for longer stays. Adds amenities like **deluxe cabins**, group meeting facilities, and **patio RV sites**.
- **KOA Resort:** Offers a destination experience with a combination of additional amenities like a **pool**, **dog park**, restaurant, or mini-golf.

> [!WARNING]
> These tiers refer to the **type of amenities** offered, not the **quality or price** of the campground. You can find an impeccable KOA Journey or a run-down KOA Resort, and their prices can vary just as much.

## Is It Worth It? Pricing & Rewards

### Pricing
Before concluding a KOA is too expensive, it's crucial to compare it fairly.

> [!TIP]
> Compare a KOA's price to other **local, full-hookup campgrounds with similar amenities**. Often, the pricing is comparable for what's offered.

### KOA Rewards Program
- **Cost:** **$36 per year**.
- **Benefit:** **10% discount** on the daily registration rate.
- **Is it worth it?** It's a simple math problem. If you plan to spend more than **$360** at KOA campgrounds in a year, the program pays for itself.
- It is a **loyalty program**, not a required membership to stay at a KOA.

## Final Takeaway: Judge Each Park Individually
The most important advice is to treat KOA campgrounds just like any other independent commercial park.

- **Avoid brand loyalty or blanket aversion.**
- **Do your research for each specific location:**
  - Check recent reviews on sites like **CampgroundReviews.com** and **Google Maps**.
  - Compare the park's specific amenities and price against other local options to find the best fit for your needs.
transcription:
## Debunking KOA Campground Myths

KOA Campgrounds, what's the big deal? Are they a great place to stay or are they overpriced sardine cans?

We're going to get into all the nitty-gritty about camping at KOA Campgrounds, some things that people might not know about in this video. This is RV miles. Hi everybody, welcome back to RV miles. Today I wanted to dive into the largest Campground chain in North America, KOA. A lot of people have opinions on KOA Campgrounds: they're too expensive, they're always charging extra, their sites are too close together, they're okay but they're reliable, you have to buy a membership to use one, they're always by the railroad tracks, whatever it might be.

So right off the bat, I want to say that many opinions about KOA are just wrong, whether they're bad or good or in between. And that's because KOA, or Campgrounds of America, is a fairly loose franchise organization. And the vast majority of their 500 plus locations are owned and operated by individual franchisees who set their own prices, have their own rules, and take care of their own facilities.

If you have a pretty strong belief about KOA after a visit to one or two, it's possible that the next one you visit will challenge that belief, good or bad. I think KOA corporate operates less than 20 of their locations overall, so most KOAs are run by small local business owners.

## The History and Evolution of KOA

KOA Campgrounds have been around for over 60 years and its founding was really the invention of the modern commercial campground. In the early 1960s, Dave Drum noticed an abundance of station wagons and early model RVs overnighting on the side of the road or in church and retail parking lots. Dave owned some land along the Yellowstone River in his hometown of Billings, Montana, where he installed electric hookups, central shower facilities, and a convenience store. KOA's headquarters is in Billings to this day. Two years later, the first KOA franchise was established not too far away in Cody, Wyoming, and then they began to spread about the country.

Dave collaborated with a local artist to create the iconic KOA logo, which has never changed. And because they weren't allowed to trademark the word 'Campground' as part of the name, they replaced the C with a K and Campgrounds of America was born. Now you may think there are 500-plus campgrounds across Canada and the US is a lot, but KOA's expansion throughout the 70s and into the 80s was massive. At their peak, there were over 900 active KOA Campgrounds.

A lot of commercial campgrounds, including KOAs, closed during the oil crisis that happened in the late 70s, early 80s. People really weren't traveling on the roads back then. KOA's size, though, allowed it to hang on but not without some ownership changes and some casualties. Many KOA franchises also changed hands. They closed or left the organization over the years, and that's why you'll see the occasional campground that has the traditional A-frame main building that's such a KOA signature that are no longer a KOA Campground.

## Sponsor: RVmattress.com by Brooklyn Bedding

More in a moment, but first, this video is sponsored by rvmattress.com by Brooklyn Bedding. Our friends at rvmattress.com make real mattresses for people to put in their RVs that replace the pieces of junk. There's all these mattresses that they're putting in in RVs right now that are supposed to be greener; they're made out of a biodegradable recyclable material. That's because they expect them to be thrown away. They're essentially ramen noodles. They're not good for sleeping on. If you want to be comfortable in your RV, if it didn't come with a good mattress, rvmattress.com by Brooklyn Bedding offers real mattresses that you get shipped to you vacuum packed into a box through the mail.

They even have hybrid mattresses with springs inside them that still come through the mail, and you can get them in lots of different sizes to fit that short queen or short king or the not fully King that they are putting in RVs for some reason these days. They have twin mattresses and bunk mattress sizes. They have different thicknesses and they are great. We have them in both of our RVs, we have them in our house, and we love sleeping on mattresses from Brooklyn Bedding because they're legit. It's not some piece of foam that you bought off the Internet, it's a real mattress. They have a 120-night sleep trial, a 10-year warranty. Their mattresses are made in their Factory in Arizona and shipped to you Factory Direct from there. And you can even get them in campgrounds and you just open them up, let them expand, and you're all ready to sleep for the night. RV Miles viewers get 25% off when you visit rvmattress.com/RVMiles and use the code RVMILES at checkout.

## The KOA Franchise Business Model

Now as I said before, KOAs can be very different, but they do have to meet some standards to be a franchise. Sometimes existing campgrounds join into the KOA system, but often their parks are new construction. And that's because KOA really makes it simpler for a prospective campground owner to navigate all the hurdles of campground design and construction, zoning and approvals, and software and management training. A new KOA Campground franchise has to have at least 75 RV sites and 90 total sites. Those extras might be cabins or they might be tent-only sites. The average cost to build a KOA Campground is between 3.9 and $6.8 million, not including the cost of the land.

They have to pay an initial franchise fee of $40,000, which gets them consulting and campground design assistance, a KOA sign package, training for management at KOA University in Billings, and access to K2, their proprietary management software for registrations and reservations. After that, they pay a $1,700 annual fee and have to give 10% of their annual revenue to KOA corporate for royalties and marketing. But they are a marketing behemoth, and that's why a lot of owners join KOA, because the name gets them people in the door. But it can be expensive to operate a KOA franchise, which can cause the price to creep up a bit. But a lot of owners do it because it takes the hassle out of doing some of those things themselves that also would have cost money. And it can also be expensive to operate the competing campground across the street.

## Are KOA Campgrounds Overpriced?

This is why I always say when people comment that KOAs are too expensive, and they do every time I do a video that has any mention of KOA: sure, but compared to what? Compared to the full hookup campground with similar amenities in the same town? It's often about the same, or at least it's all over the place. We've been to areas where KOAs were absurdly expensive compared to the competition and others where they're the most affordable option. Most of the time, it's pretty comparable.

I think a lot of people, especially when they're new to camping, though, really like to go to KOAs because they think they're going to get at least a base level of customer service and amenities. There's a lot of people that say, "I only camp at KOAs." There's a lot of like Canadians that come down to the US and they plan their entire trip based on going to KOAs because they feel like they know what they're going to get. But the problem is with KOAs, since it's a fairly loose franchise, that's not exactly true. We've been to some absolutely terrible ones, some great ones, and everything in between.

## KOA Journey, Holiday, and Resort Tiers Explained

That said, KOA does monitor their campground and they do expect their owners to live up to a certain level of quality. And KOA has tried to do some things to manage expectations from customers too, because really, there are all types of campgrounds out there, and KOA has all types of campgrounds within their system.

A few years ago, KOA divided the campgrounds in their system into three categories: Journey, Holiday, and Resort. KOA Journey campgrounds are at a minimum sort of the overnight stopover style. That doesn't mean they can't be a great base camp, but they don't have a lot of frills. They're supposed to have pull-through RV sites, 50-amp electrical hookups, premium tent sites, clean bathrooms with hot water, laundry facilities, a playground, and a KOA store.

A KOA Holiday throws in cabins into the mix, along with patio RV sites and facilities for group meetings. A KOA Resort will have some combination of additional amenities like a dog park, a restaurant, a game room, a pool, mini golf, fishing, et cetera. So for an owner to get into those categories, sometimes it can be an expense. So if you want to be a KOA Holiday, well, you got to build some cabins, you've got to build these patio RV sites, and that can add to the overall cost of running a KOA. And of course that can add to the cost of you visiting a KOA.

But overall, I think these categories—the Journey, the Holiday—I don't think they're very important to the customer as much as KOA would like to think that they are. They don't really refer to the quality or the price of the campground. You can have a rundown KOA Resort or an impeccable KOA Journey. You can have an expensive KOA Journey and an affordable KOA Resort. It's really all over the place.

## The KOA Rewards Loyalty Program

KOA offers a loyalty program called KOA Rewards. A lot of people wonder if they should buy into it when they start out RVing. It's $36 a year and it gets you 10% off stays at KOA. So really, it's just a math thing. If you expect you'll recoup the $36, you should buy it. If not, there's no reason to. A lot of people think you have to become members; you don't. It's really just a loyalty program like joining Walmart Plus or Target Circle.

## Final Verdict: How to Choose a KOA

So really, I think the big thing I wanted to get across in this video is that you should treat KOAs like any other commercial campground. They're just as different and varied as all the other parks out there. And when you choose somewhere to stay, you check reviews on places like CampgroundReviews.com or even just reviews on Google. Look at the amenities and compare them with other options available to you and decide if it's the best place for you or not.

There's really no reason to get into the brand loyalty of KOA or to be kind of snobbish about not wanting to go to one unless you avoid commercial campgrounds altogether, which is totally fine. I'd love to know in the comments your thoughts on KOA Campgrounds. Have you stayed at one lately? Where, and how was it? Please hit the like button if you got something out of this video. Subscribe if you want more like this, and we'll see you on the next one. Thanks, everybody.
